To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

negative priming (the effect that occurs when a stimulus that was ignored in a prior task interferes with processing on a subsequent trial) results in increased activation of a region of the right dorsalateral prefrontal (DLPFC) that has been linked to episodic retrieval, and increased activation of the thalamus, especially the mediodorsa nucleus (MD), which has been implicated with the pathophysiology schizophrenia.

(1) negative priming (i.e. a delay in the processing of an ignored stimulus on a current trial due to its prior occurrence as a target on a previous trial) is a function of episodic retrieval, rather than selective inhibition of the ignored stimulus on the prior trial, and (2) the right thalamo-dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex circuit, which has previously been linked to episodic memory retrieval, is involved in the generation of negative priming.

the negative priming ( NP ) effect refers to the increased identification time for a target stimulus that has been employed in a previous trial as a distractor, representing strong evidence that attended information is actively processed by selective attention systems, and the key findings of this research are that compared to no priming probe trials, negative priming resulted in increased activation in the right dorsolatera prefrontal cortex and right thalamus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of attentional control and memory retrieval processes.
the neural mechanisms underlying the ability to selectively attend to one stimulus at a time.
the neural mechanisms of attention and memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the negative priming effect is the result of a combination of episodic memory retrieval and selective attention processes.
negative priming is a result of episodic retrieval of the ignored prime.
the NP effect is a function of the episodic memory system, which is involved in the retrieval of the previous prime stimulus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the negative priming effect is a function of the episodic retrieval of ignored stimulus information, and that this retrieval occurs within a right-hemisphere attention network.
the right dorsolaterl prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and the right thalamo-cortical circuitry are important for the negative priming effect.
the right dorsolaterl prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and the right mediodorsal thalamus (MD) are involved in the episodic retrieval process of the negative priming effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have provided the first neurophysiological evidence that the neural mechanisms underlying negative priming are related to memory retrieval processes, and not selective inhibition.
we can use the negative priming effect to understand the neural substrates of memory and attention.
we were able to show, using a novel experimental design and neuroimaging techniques, how the neural systems involved in memory retrieval and selective attention are closely linked.
